text:
Now I move to the third paper in the dissertation.
If the first paper studies belief formation and the second studies reliance calibration, this paper asks what happens once a consequential action has to be owned.
The core question is not simply whether AI is used.
It is whether AI system design changes who feels accountable for the final move before the outcome is even known.

text:
I want to begin with a concrete decision scene rather than with theory.
In more and more high-risk settings, people do not decide alone anymore. They see an AI analysis before they act, and sometimes they must confirm or disclose how they used it.
That means the key shift is not only what information enters the room.
It is also whether the final choice still feels fully like my own decision.

text:
The literature is not empty. In fact, it is already quite rich.
But most studies isolate one piece at a time: trust in AI, delegation to another decision agent, or blame once the outcome is already known.
What remains underdeveloped is the process question.
How does responsibility design inside an AI-supported system change risky choice before the outcome arrives?

text:
The point here is not to reject traditional theory.
Rationalist conflict theory and behavioral risk theory both help us understand escalation.
But they usually start from the assumption that responsibility cost is already given in the environment.
What AI support may change is exactly that background condition: the accountability structure itself.

text:
This slide condenses the literature critique into one visual field.
The problem is not that nobody studies AI responsibility.
The problem is that most work stays at the level of attribution after the outcome, or treats AI participation as one coarse condition.
My question is more design-specific: which interventions inside an AI-supported process actually change ownership, accountability, and risky action before the outcome is known?

These questions all push in the same direction.
Instead of treating AI support as one broad treatment, I ask whether different responsibility designs change how the human actor experiences final agency.
That is why the questions move from AI support itself, to ownership and felt accountability, and then back to behavior.

This slide prevents an obvious misunderstanding.
The broader theory does speak in terms of AI moving closer to action, but the present experiment does not claim to operationalize every role position at once.
Instead, it focuses on two concrete interventions inside the same AI-supported decision process: confirm and disclosure.

text:
This slide explains why the experimental environment is appropriate before we get lost in design detail.
Hawk-Dove is useful because escalation is not just a generic risk preference. It is a consequential move with external loss if both sides escalate.
The flow on the right then makes the design transparent: keep the strategic environment fixed, vary the responsibility architecture inside the process, and observe behavior.

This is the most valuable method page in the deck.
The point is to let the committee see, in one field, how each research question maps onto a manipulation, what comparison identifies it, and what mechanism that contrast is supposed to isolate.
That is what keeps the experiment from collapsing into a vague AI-versus-no-AI design.

I end by emphasizing that the contribution is not another generic claim about trust in AI.
The contribution is to identify where responsibility changes inside an AI-supported decision process, and to test whether those changes can be seen in behavior before outcomes arrive.
That is what makes Paper 3 the responsibility link in the larger dissertation architecture.
